paragraphs: Ignorance, and the misguided cunning that nature sharpens in weak heads as a means of self-preservation, make women very fond of dress, and produce all the vanity that such a fondness may naturally be expected to breed, to the exclusion of emulation and greatness of spirit.

I agree with Rousseau that the physical part of the art of pleasing consists in ornaments; and for that very reason I would guard girls against the infectious love of dress so common among weak women, so that they do not stop at the physical part. Yet weak indeed are the women who imagine that they can please for long without the help of the mind — in other words, without the moral art of pleasing. But the moral art (if it is not a profanation to use the word “art” for the grace that is an effect of virtue, not a motive of action) is never found together with ignorance. The playfulness of innocence, so pleasing to refined libertines of both sexes, differs widely in its essence from this higher gracefulness.

A strong liking for outward ornament always shows itself in barbarous states, except that there it is the men and not the women who adorn themselves; for where women are allowed to stand so nearly level with men, society has advanced at least one step in civilization.

The attention to dress, therefore, which has been thought a peculiarly female inclination, I consider natural to mankind. But I ought to express myself more precisely. When the mind is not open enough to take pleasure in reflection, the body will be adorned with painstaking care, and ambition will show itself in tattooing or painting it.

This first inclination is carried so far that even the hellish yoke of slavery cannot stifle the savage craving for admiration which the black heroes inherit from both their parents; for all the hard-earned savings of a slave are commonly spent on a little tawdry finery. And I have seldom known a good servant, male or female, who was not particularly fond of dress. Their clothes were their wealth; and I argue by analogy that the love of dress, so extravagant in women, springs from the same cause — a lack of cultivation of the mind. When men meet, they talk about business, politics or literature; but, says Swift, “how naturally do women apply their hands to each others lappets and ruffles.” And very natural it is — for they have no business to interest them, they have no taste for literature, and they find politics dry, because they have not acquired a love of mankind by turning their thoughts to the grand pursuits that raise the human race and promote general happiness.

Besides, men pursue many different paths to power and fame, whether by chance or by choice; and though they jostle one another, since men of the same profession are seldom friends, there is still a far greater number of their fellow creatures with whom they never clash. But women stand in a very different position towards one another — for they are all rivals.

Before marriage their business is to please men; and afterwards, with a few exceptions, they follow the same scent with all the dogged persistence of instinct. Even virtuous women never forget their sex in company, for they are forever trying to make themselves AGREEABLE. A female beauty and a male wit seem equally anxious to draw the attention of the company to themselves; and the hostility between wits of the same generation is proverbial.

Is it surprising, then, that when a woman’s sole ambition centres on beauty, and self-interest gives vanity extra force, endless rivalries should follow? They are all running the same race, and they would have to rise above mortal virtue not to look at one another with a suspicious and even envious eye.

An immoderate love of dress, of pleasure and of power are the passions of savages — the passions that occupy those uncivilized beings who have not yet extended the rule of the mind, or even learned to think with the energy needed to link together the abstract chain of thought that produces principles. And that women, because of their education and the present state of civilized life, are in the same condition cannot, I think, be denied. To laugh at them, then, or to satirize the follies of a being who is never allowed to act freely by the light of her own reason, is as absurd as it is cruel; for it is most natural and certain that those who are taught to obey authority blindly will try to evade it by cunning.

Yet let it be proved that they ought to obey man without question, and I will at once agree that it is woman’s duty to cultivate a love of dress in order to please, and a tendency to cunning for her own protection.

The virtues that rest on ignorance, however, must always waver — the house built on sand could not withstand a storm. There is hardly any need to draw the inference. If women are to be made virtuous by authority, which is a contradiction in terms, let them be walled up in harems and watched with a jealous eye. Do not fear that the iron will enter their souls — for souls that can bear such treatment are made of pliant stuff, just alive enough to animate the body.
“Matter too soft a lasting mark to bear, And best distinguish’d by black, brown, or fair.”

The cruellest wounds will naturally soon heal, and they may still populate the world and dress to please man — which are all the purposes that certain celebrated writers have granted they were created to serve.

Women are supposed to have more sensibility, and even more humanity, than men, and their strong attachments and sudden rushes of compassion are offered as proof. But the clinging affection of ignorance seldom has anything noble in it, and can mostly be reduced to selfishness, like the affection of children and animals. I have known many weak women whose sensibility was wholly absorbed by their husbands; and as for their humanity, it was very faint indeed, or rather it was only a passing feeling of compassion. “Humanity does not consist in a squeamish ear,” says an eminent orator. “It belongs to the mind as well as the nerves.”

But this kind of exclusive affection, though it degrades the individual, should not be put forward as proof of the inferiority of the sex, because it is the natural result of narrow views. For even women of superior good sense, with their attention directed to small occupations and private plans, seldom rise to heroism except when spurred on by love; and love as a heroic passion, like genius, appears only once in an age. I therefore agree with the moralist who asserts “that women have seldom so much generosity as men;” and that their narrow affections, to which justice and humanity are often sacrificed, make the sex seem inferior, especially as those affections are commonly inspired by men. But I maintain that the heart would expand as the understanding grew stronger, if women were not held down from the cradle.

I know that a little sensibility combined with great weakness will produce a strong sexual attachment, and that it takes reason to cement friendship. I therefore grant that more friendship is found among men than among women, and that men have a higher sense of justice. The exclusive affections of women do indeed seem to resemble Cato’s most unjust love for his country. He wanted to crush Carthage, not to save Rome but to promote its vainglory; and in general it is to similar principles that humanity is sacrificed, for genuine duties support one another.
Besides, how can women be just or generous when they are the slaves of injustice?
